title: What is the intuition behind the KL constraint in the RLHF objective (Eq. 3)?
question_body:
In the RL fine-tuning objective (Eq. 3),
$$
\max_{\pi_\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},y\sim\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}[r_\phi(x,y)]\;-
\beta\,D_{KL}(\pi_\theta(\cdot|x)\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|x)).
$$
I understand the reward maximization term, but why is the KL divergence term necessary? Conceptually, what pathologies or instabilities does it prevent during policy fine-tuning?

title: How does DPO reparameterization avoid computing the partition function $Z(x)$?
question_body:
The paper claims that by reparameterizing the reward via Eq. 5,
$$
r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_r(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)}+\beta\log Z(x),
$$
we can cancel $Z(x)$ out when forming preference probabilities. Could someone walk through how substituting this into the Bradley–Terry model (Eq. 1) eliminates the partition function?

title: How should I choose the reference policy $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ in practice for DPO?
question_body: DPO requires a fixed reference model $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ (often the SFT model). How sensitive is DPO to this choice? If I only have preference data but no SFT model, how do I train or choose $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ to minimize distribution shift?

title: What is the role of the hyperparameter $\beta$ in DPO?
question_body: The DPO loss (Eq. 7) and gradient (Eq. 8) both depend on a scaling parameter $\beta$. Intuitively, how does $\beta$ affect the trade-off between adhering to preferences and staying close to $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$? Is it directly analogous to the temperature in Eq. 4?

title: In the DPO gradient (Eq. 8), why is there a weighting term $\sigma(\hat r_\theta(y_l)-\hat r_\theta(y_w))$?
question_body:
The paper emphasizes that the gradient includes
$$
\sigma\bigl(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)\bigr)
$$
as an importance weight. What is the intuition for this factor, and what issues arise if we drop it (i.e., use an unweighted likelihood ratio update)?
